description:
**Top Trending Friday** — our weekly pick of the top-trending paper on r/science this week.

**[Not with a Bang but a Whimper: Congressional Silence Amid an Historic Assault on the Power of the Purse](https://doi.org/10.1017/S1049096525101704)**

*PS: Political Science & Politics, 2025*

DOI: [10.1017/S1049096525101704](https://doi.org/10.1017/S1049096525101704)

**Question:** Why has Congress barely resisted President Trump's unilateral impoundments and tariffs, actions that assault its constitutional power of the purse?

**Answer:** Kriner argues partisan incentives and Trump's dominance of his party have muted congressional pushback, despite public opposition and statutory violations. It's an analytic case essay, not a measured dataset, so the "historic" comparison and the proposed mechanism remain largely narrative.

**Three takeaways**

1. The core claim—Congress acted less than historical precedent—lacks a counted baseline (hearings, riders, votes) across administrations; it's asserted, not measured.
2. Under unified government, partisanship and institutional erosion predict identical silence, so the paper can't separate which mechanism is driving it.
3. The durable point: the 1974 Impoundment Control Act has no self-executing enforcement, so a Congress unwilling to use it leaves the statute toothless.

source_metadata.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  Although all presidents pursue their agendas unilaterally, President Donald Trump’s early second-term actions shocked the political system for their scope and breadth. One of Trump’s boldest moves was a frontal assault on Congress’s constitutional power of the purse through unprecedented impoundments and unilateral tariffs. Despite widespread public opposition to Trump’s gambits and clear statutory violations, Congress has offered little resistance, marking a stark departure from historical precedent. This analysis situates Trump’s actions within broader debates over the scope of executive authority and the weakening of institutional checks and balances. Partisan incentives and Trump’s dominance of the Republican Party have muted congressional resistance, raising urgent questions about the future of the separation of powers in an era of unprecedented executive overreach.
